paper_title: HERA: Harness-Environment Co-Evolution for Reliable Agentic Abstention

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of acting in complex tool-use environments, yet they often fail to recognize when tasks are infeasible and no valid solution exists. Recent work has formalized this reliability gap as the problem of agentic abstention, and existing approaches typically optimize a model or agent harness against a fixed set of tasks, leading to limited generalization to unseen failure modes. We introduce HERA, a framework for harness-environment co-evolution for agentic abstention. HERA consists of (i) a pipeline to automatically construct verifiable pairs of feasible and infeasible tasks by applying controlled environment mutations that transform solvable tasks into cases requiring abstention, and (ii) a co-evolution procedure in which performance failures on previous tasks are used to drive harness adaptation and generate new execution environments and tasks geared towards previous weaknesses. On held-out evaluation tasks, an evolved harness from HERA improves abstention accuracy from 61.7% to 83.3% while improving feasible-task completion from 68.3% to 76.7%, achieving the highest abstention and feasible-task completion among the compared methods. The resulting best harness transfers across 19 other LLMs, improving abstention accuracy by 15.3 percentage points on average without any model-specific optimization, and enabling smaller models to match the performance of more powerful models at an estimated 85% lower cost.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of solving complex tasks through multi-step interactions with tools and external environments (Merrill et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2022), yet their reliability still lags behind in many areas. Recent work on agent reliability has identified agentic abstention (Luo et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) as key challenge: agents often fail to recognize when they should stop and instead continue acting even when request is underspecified or the environment lacks the prerequisites for successful execution. This ability to recognize appropriate stopping is essential, as continuing to act when task cannot or should not be completed can degrade task performance (Wan et al., 2026; Sui et al., 2026), incur unnecessary API costs and latency (Lou et al., 2026), and even lead to unintended or irreversible actions (Zhang et al., 2026a). Prior work has improved agent capability through (i) methods that optimize the model directly, e.g., through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or online policy optimization (Agarwal et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b;a), and (ii) methods that keep the model fixed and instead optimize the agent harness around it, which governs context construction, memory and skills, tool use, action validation, and the control logic for continuing, recovering, or stopping execution (Shao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Karten et al., 2026). The former has received considerable attention, whereas the role of harness optimization in agentic abstention remains largely unexplored. Optimizing harness against fixed set of tasks can only expose limited set of failures. As the harness adapts to failures exposed by those tasks, the same examples provide diminishing signal about Equal contribution. 1 where the harness still fails. Continued improvement requires the task distribution itself to adapt, evolving new cases that challenge existing capabilities. This idea parallels recent work on adaptive data generation, in which model performance is used to iteratively refine the data-generation process and expose new learning opportunities (Meng et al., 2026). For agentic abstention, we therefore consider setting in which harness optimization and environment/task generation co-evolve, where agent failures shape improvements to the harness and elicit more challenging tasks for the agent. This is the primary motivation for our work. We introduce HERA, framework for harnessenvironment co-evolution for agentic abstention. HERA proceeds in two stages. In Stage 1, building on methods from Dong et al. (2026), we construct executable environments and tasks with verified reference solutions. We then introduce new environment-mutation procedure for constructing infeasible tasks, transforming feasible tasks into matched cases requiring abstention. Each pair of feasible-infeasible tasks shares the same task request, while the environment mutation determines whether the request can be completed. In Stage 2, using the task data construction procedure in Stage 1, HERA alternates environment evolution and new task construction with harness adaptation. For each round of co-evolution, we analyze paired execution trajectories to identify both failures to complete feasible tasks and failures to abstain on infeasible tasks. These failures guide targeted harness changes to environment states, tool behavior, or constraints, followed by new environment-task modification and validation. After each round, an updated harness provides failure feedback for the next round, allowing environment generation to respond to the agents changing weaknesses and vice versa. We use HERA to produce challenging evaluation set for agentic abstention, which we call HERABENCH. We then execute HERA using GPT-5.6-Luna as our base task-execution model. We apply the final evolved harness across 19 other LLMs on HERA-BENCH, where it improves abstention and paired success by an average of 15.3 and 12.5 percentage points, respectively, without further model-specific optimizations. We further analyze inference costs for 14 models and find that, despite the additional overhead of the evolved harness, HERA can enable less expensive models to achieve comparable performance to more costly models at significantly lower overall cost. We also compare HERA against baselines such as abstention prompting, harness-only optimization, and alternative task-expansion strategies. Each methods final harness is evaluated on our cumulative training pool and HERA-BENCH. Across cumulative training sets, HERA matches or outperforms all compared baselines, reaching 86.0% abstention success and 78.0% paired success on the final 50pair pool. On HERA-BENCH, HERA improves abstention success from 61.7% to 83.3% and paired success from 48.3% to 70.0% relative to the base harness. In summary, our key contributions are as follows: Benchmark for agentic abstention. As part of HERA, we introduce controlled environmentmutation pipeline for constructing matched feasibleinfeasible task pairs in executable tool-use environments, where infeasible instances require the agent to abstain. Using this pipeline, we construct HERA-BENCH, benchmark of 60 verified task pairs for evaluating whether agents appropriately act when tasks are feasible and abstain when they are infeasible. Harnessenvironment co-evolution. HERA then combines verifiable task construction with failure-driven environment evolution and harness adaptation. On the final training pool, HERA achieves 86.0% abstention success and 78.0% paired success, exceeding the next-best baseline by 10.0 percentage points on both metrics. These results support the necessity of both harness and environment/task updates, as well as multiple iterations for both. Transferable improvements in agentic abstention. On held-out tasks in HERA-BENCH, the final harness from HERA increases abstention success from 61.7% to 83.3% and paired success from 48.3% to 70.0%. Across 19 additional LLMs, the same final harness improves these metrics by an average of 15.3 and 12.5 percentage points without further optimization. These findings indicate that harness improvements generalize beyond the model used during development. Performancecost trade-offs. We analyze API costs and token usage across 14 models, examining the additional inference overhead of harness adaptation and differences between model configurations. HERA enables less expensive models to achieve performance gains approaching more costly models. For example, GPT-5.6-Luna with HERA matches the 70.0% paired success of base GPT-6-Astra at an estimated 85% lower API cost per episode.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Agentic Abstention. LLM abstention is defined as models decision to refrain from answering under uncertainty (Wen et al., 2025; Kirichenko et al., 2025; Wen et al.; 2024). Existing studies of LLM abstention can be broadly grouped by why abstention is warranted: insufficient information in the query or available context (Cao et al., 2026; Kwiatkowski et al., 2019; Trivedi et al., 2022; Reddy et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; Min et al., 2020; Zhang & Choi, 2021; Yin et al., 2023; Amayuelas et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2019; Dasigi et al., 2021), limitations in the models knowledge due to temporal or factual gaps (Kasai et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Mallen et al., 2023; Sciavolino et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2024), and safety or value concerns that make responding inappropriate (Han et al., 2024; Gehman et al., 2020; Hartvigsen et al., 2022; ElSherief et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Rottger et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; 2023; Li et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). Recent work has begun to shift the study of abstention from LLMs to agent settings. Luo et al. (2026) first introduce the notion of agentic abstention, asking whether agents know when to stop instead of act, and evaluate this capability across QA, web, and terminal environments. They find that current agents often fail to identify when abstention is warranted. Liu et al. (2026) similarly study agentic abstention by constructing executable environmenttask pairs, where controlled changes to tasks or environments create cases in which agents should abstain rather than act. Relatedly, (Lin et al., 2026b) study closely related stopping problem through the lens of budget awareness, asking whether agents can estimate their remaining resource requirements and identify when task completion is unlikely within the available budget. However, the environments in these works are fixed or generated independently of agent performance, whereas we use agent failures to drive environment generation and the resulting environments to iteratively improve the agent harness. Harness Evolution. Prior work improves agents by optimizing individual parts of the external scaffold, including prompts, demonstrations, and language-model programs. (Khattab et al., 2023; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2026). More recent work treats the full agent harness as the object of optimization. Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) searches over harness code using execution feedback, while Agentic Harness Engineering (Lin et al., 2026a) jointly evolves components such as prompts, tools, middleware, skills, and memory, and AEVO (Zhang et al., 2026c) optimizes the procedure and context that guide subsequent agent evolution. Recent approaches further explore harness improvement through failure-driven self-refinement (Zhang et al., 2026b), learned runtime editing (Shao et al., 2026), more reliable search and generalization (Zhang et al., 2026d), and population-based evolution (Zhang et al., 2026e). Task-CoEvolve (Miyai et al., 2026) additionally adapts the selection of validation tasks as the harness changes, while recent work has also questioned whether gains from harness evolution generalize beyond the tasks repeatedly used during optimization (Wang et al., 2026). Unlike prior harness-evolution methods, which typically improve the harness against fixed environments, we evolve the harness together with the environmenttask ecosystem, adapting the latter to target weaknesses exposed by the current harness. We apply this idea to agentic abstention.

sections.title: 3 METHODOLOGY: HARNESS-ENVIRONMENT CO-EVOLUTION
sections.content: In this section, we describe the two stages of HERA, (i) how we construct and verify feasible and infeasible tasks (3.1) and (ii) how these task pairs are then used to adapt the harness and generate new and more challenging environments (3.2). 3.1 VERIFIABLE ABSTENTION ENVIRONMENTTASK CONSTRUCTION Our first stage constructs diverse and executable environmenttask ecosystems from scratch. The pipeline consists of three steps: environment construction, task generation, and environment mutation (further details and illustration in Appendix A.1). Environment construction. As in Dong et al. (2026), we begin with diverse collection of environment themes, where each specifies semantic domain from which an interactive environment is constructed. For each theme, we construct topic-aligned structured database using deep-research agent with fixed research policy and set of research tools. The initial database is iteratively expanded and refined to accumulate more structured information. After database construction, we 3 Figure 1: Harnessenvironment co-evolution. Given an environment pool of feasible and infeasible tasks and current harness, paired rollouts and failure diagnosis are used to iteratively evolve both the environment pool and harness. Environment evolution (top) constructs, validates, and selects new feasibleinfeasible task pairs to challenge the current agent and expand the training pool. Harness evolution (bottom) similarly refines the harness iteratively on the expanded task pool, with each updated harness selected from candidates using performance on validation set. synthesize an executable interface over the resulting data. bounded coding procedure, operating under tool-generation policy, produces candidate tool set. We subsequently validate the generated tools against the underlying database, filtering out tools that are non-executable or inconsistent with the database schema. The resulting executable environment is denoted by Eθ. Task generation. Given constructed environment Eθ, task proposer generates candidate tasks grounded in the available data and tool capabilities. To avoid having the same model both propose and judge its own tasks, we use an independent solver to attempt each task through the public tool interface. We retain only tasks that can be successfully completed and validated in the environment and denote the resulting set of validated tasks by Qθ. This step both filters out infeasible candidates and produces executable reference trajectories that are later used to assess how environment mutations change task feasibility. Environment mutation. For each pair (Eθ, Qθ), we instantiate independent proposers to generate diverse pool of candidate mutation proposals. Using multiple proposers reduces dependence on single generation trajectory and increases the diversity of possible environment modifications. Candidate proposals are reviewed by two complementary policies. The semantic policy πsem evaluates whether proposed mutation remains semantically consistent with the underlying task and environment, while the rescue policy πres examines whether the task can still be completed through an unintended alternative route despite the proposed modification. Together, these policies form proposal-validation gate. Proposals that do not satisfy the validation criteria are sent through proposal-refinement loop and reviewed again. Let θ denote proposal that successfully passes this review. The mutation operator then applies it to the original environment: θ) . See θ = M(Eθ; The resulting Figure 5 in Appendix A.1 for the mutation pipeline. 3.2 HARNESSENVIRONMENT CO-EVOLUTION Motivation & overview. An effective agent must be able to complete tasks when valid solution exists and recognize when the task is infeasible. Our goal is to improve abstention on infeasible cases without sacrificing task-solving capability and, where possible, strengthen both. Following prior work on feedback-driven harness evolution (Lin et al., 2026a), we use execution trajectories and task outcomes to guide iterative updates to the agents harness. HERA extends this process by coupling harness optimization with failure-guided evolution of executable environments and matched 4 feasibleinfeasible task pairs, allowing the training pool to adapt to the current harness. The verifiable environmenttask pairs constructed in Section 3.1 serve as both training tasks and diagnostics for failures in task solving and abstention. These failures guide harness improvements and the targeted construction of new environmenttask pairs, which in turn expose new weaknesses in the updated harness. Repeating this process forms harnessenvironment co-evolution loop, where the harness adapts to the challenges it encounters while the environments evolve to target its current weaknesses. Figure 1 provides an overview of the harnessenvironment co-evolution process. At the beginning of each co-evolution round, we maintain an environment pool Eg and an agent equipped with the current harness Hk. Each member of the pool is shared task instruction and its matched feasible and infeasible environments, corresponding to the Act and Abstain cases, respectively. We execute the agent on both tasks in the pair and collect the resulting trajectories Rk. An LLM-based failure analyst examines these trajectories and their evaluation outcomes to identify failures in task completion and abstention. The analyst groups these failures by their underlying causes, producing structured diagnosis Fk that guides both environment evolution and harness evolution. Each round of environment and harness evolution proceeds as follows. Environment evolution. For environments in which the current agent fails to abstain appropriately, an environment designer uses the failure diagnosis Fk to modify the underlying data, tool behavior, or constraints of the parent environment P. The redesigned environment is then passed to the task-generation and environment-mutation stages of Section 3.1. Importantly, Fk also guides the proposers in both stages, so that environment design, task generation, and environment mutation jointly target the diagnosed weaknesses. The newly generated feasibleinfeasible pairs undergo certification through the same verification checks as before, which confirm an executable solution for the feasible instance and infeasibility for the abstention instance. This forms new candidate batch of feasibleinfeasible task pairs, which are then evaluated with the current harness version Hk. The batch is admitted to the next evolution round if the proportion of infeasible instances on which the agent fails to abstain appropriately is above predefined threshold τ . If so, we retain the entire batch, including some instances that the current harness already handles correctly, and add it to the cumulative training pool. If the batch does not meet the threshold, it is revised or replaced with new candidate batch. Harness evolution. Given the updated training pool Eg+1, we first evaluate the agent with the current harness Hk on all instances and derive fresh failure diagnosis Fk,0. We then evolve the harness over update steps. The harness optimizer may modify prompts, memory, sub-agents, skills, tools, and control logic while keeping the underlying language model fixed. Formally, we initialize Hk,0 = Hk and generate successive candidates as: Hk,i+1 = Optimize(Hk,i, Fk,i), = 0, . . . , 1. (2) Each candidate harness is evaluated through paired training rollouts over the entire pool Eg+1. The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are analyzed to derive an updated failure diagnosis Fk,i+1, which guides the next update. Each update builds directly on the preceding candidate, regardless of whether that candidate improves performance. The training pool remains fixed throughout all updates. After completing the sequence, we compare all candidates with the round-start harness Hk on fixed validation set. This set is disjoint from all cumulative training pools and from HERA-BENCH, and remains unchanged across co-evolution rounds. We use two metrics for this comparison: Abstain, the fraction of infeasible instances on which the agent correctly abstains, and Pair, the fraction of matched pairs for which the agent both successfully completes the feasible instance and correctly abstains on the infeasible instance. candidate is eligible for adoption only if neither metric decreases relative to Hk on the same validation set and at least one strictly improves. We select the best eligible candidate as Hk+1; if none qualifies, we retain Hk. Validation results are used only for final checkpoint selection and are not provided as feedback to the harness optimizer.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Our experiments address three questions: (1) Can harnessenvironment co-evolution improve agentic abstention without increasing refusals on feasible tasks? (2) How do harness evolution and 5 environment evolution separately contribute to performance? And (3) as the task pool grows, do successive harnesses improve on new tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones? Training and evaluation data. We initialize the training pool with 20 task-pairs (20 feasible, 20 infeasible) generated using our Stage 1 pipeline. During co-evolution, we introduce 30 additional task-pairs (5 each of feasible and infeasible tasks per iteration) while retaining earlier tasks, expanding the cumulative training pool from 20 to 50 task-pairs (100 total task instances). We report performance on these cumulative training pools to track adaptation to new tasks and retention of performance on earlier tasks. To assess generalization, we introduce HERA-BENCH, held-out evaluation benchmark consisting of 60 task-pairs (60 feasible, 60 infeasible). HERA-BENCH is initially generated using our environmenttask construction pipeline (3.1) on domains that are disjoint from those used for training, and subsequently manually reviewed and revised by authors to make the resulting taskenvironment pairs more natural and realistic. The review covers scenario plausibility, consistency between task instructions and environment behavior, and the validity of each feasibleinfeasible pair, as detailed in Appendix D. Harness. Our base harness, H0, is minimal tool-calling agent built on the OpenAI Agents SDK (OpenAI, 2025), with environment tools exposed through MCP. It receives task instructions and alternates between model responses and tool calls until it produces final response or reaches the 30-turn execution limit. Following prior work (Wang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a), for each round of harness evolution, we allow edits to prompts, memory, harness-level tools, skills, control logic, and sub-agent configurations. Models. We use GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026c) as our main task-execution model. We then evaluate the harness developed with GPT-5.6-Luna on 19 additional models (listed in Table 3). For each model, we compare the base harness H0 with the final evolved harness on HERA-BENCH, without further model-specific optimization. All models are evaluated with the same environment tools and scoring protocol. The detailed model list, API providers, inference settings, and execution limits are provided in Appendix A.2. Baselines. We compare HERAs co-evolution with five baselines: (i) H0 uses the original harness without adaptation; (ii) H0 + abstention prompt adds fixed abstention instruction without further harness optimization; (iii) Harness-only evolution only evolves the harness as in 3.2 without environment evolution (using only the initial set of training tasks); (iv) Task-augmented harness evolution is like (iii) except the training pool is expanded each round with more valid task-pairs generated at baseline without any environment evolution; (v) Task generation from H0 failures generates additional pairs using only H0s initial failures, then releases them in fixed batches for subsequent harness optimization. These baselines allow us to isolate the benefit of harness evolution (iii), environment evolution beyond simply adding more training tasks (iv), and continued co-evolution beyond the initial harness (v). Co-evolution parameters. We conduct co-evolution over six rounds, allowing us to observe benefits from the evolution process and approach saturation. For each round of environment evolution, we fix the batch-admission threshold at τ = 0.4 across rounds, i.e., the current harness must fail to abstain appropriately on at least two of the five infeasible instances. All tasks are retained upon acceptance. Evaluation metrics. We report the following metrics: Abstention success (Abstain): percent of infeasible tasks on which the agent correctly abstains Paired success (Pair): percent of matched task-pairs for which the agent both successfully completes the feasible instance and correctly abstains on the infeasible instance Feasible task completion (Act): percent of feasible tasks that the agent successfully completes We compare methods by reporting final harness performance on HERA-BENCH. We also conduct training dynamics analysis during co-evolution to track performance on each new task batch from its introduction onward, including measurements before and after each harness update. Starting from the base executor H0, each subsequent harness introduces or refines logic in response to diagnosed failures. H1 adds an evidence-based decision gate to distinguish recoverable uncertainty from conditions that warrant abstention; H2 introduces cross-source evidence reconciliation; H3 jointly verifies interacting task constraints before consequential actions; and H4 extends this verification to authorization relationships and cumulative privacy constraints. Green regions indicate newly introduced or refined logic relative to the preceding harness. For environment evolution, we analyze newly introduced task pairs for each round. Environment evolution introduces qualitatively different challenges over successive rounds. Some evolved tasks increase the underlying task complexity, e.g., by adding interacting constraints or more entities and relations, while others primarily make the abstention decision more difficult by changing evidence availability, permissions, or whether restrictions apply. This emphasis also shifts across rounds. We provide detailed breakdown of this analysis in Appendix E.3.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce HERA, framework for harnessenvironment co-evolution for agentic abstention. HERA constructs verifiable matched pairs of feasible and infeasible tasks through controlled environment mutations, and uses failures of the current harness to guide both subsequent environment task generation and harness adaptation. This allows the training environment to evolve alongside the agent rather than remaining fixed throughout optimization. Our experiments show that HERA substantially improves abstention while maintaining feasible task completion over the base harness and all other baselines. The resulting harness generalizes to held-out task pairs and transfers across 19 additional LLMs without model-specific optimization, yielding broad improvements in both abstention and paired success. We hope HERA provides step toward more reliable and adaptive evaluation and optimization of LLM agents.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: LLMs were used as components of the proposed framework, as described in the paper. Generative AI tools were also used to assist with implementation, analysis, and manuscript editing. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the methodology, results, and final content of the paper.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work studies agentic abstention using synthetic tasks and controlled executable environments. The study does not involve human subjects or private personal data. All experiments were conducted in controlled settings, and the authors adhered to the ICLR Code of Ethics.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We provide detailed descriptions of the framework, task and environment construction, validation procedures, and evaluation protocol in the main paper and appendices. The appendices further document implementation details, model configurations, and experimental settings used in our experiments. These materials are intended to enable reproduction of the reported results.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION AND REPRODUCIBILITY DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 ENVIRONMENTTASK CONSTRUCTION PIPELINE Figure 5 summarizes the Stage 1 pipeline used to construct verified feasibleinfeasible task pairs. Starting from set of environment themes, we first synthesize executable environments by constructing structured local database and generating corresponding tool interface, which is validated for executability and consistency with the underlying data. We then generate candidate tasks within each environment and use use GPT-5.6 Sol as an independent solver to produce and verify reference solutions, retaining only tasks that can be successfully completed. Finally, for each validated task, we generate controlled environment mutations intended to make the original request infeasible without changing the request itself. Candidate mutations are iteratively reviewed and refined using semantic checks and searches for alternative solution paths before being applied to the environment, yielding matched feasibleinfeasible pairs for downstream abstention evaluation. 15 Figure 5: End-to-End EnvironmentTask Construction Pipeline. The pipeline consists of three stages: environment construction, task generation, and environment mutation. A.2 MODELS AND INFERENCE SETTINGS Models and API access. We use GPT-5.6-Luna as the reference task-execution model during harness development and in the main experiments, and evaluate the same final harness on 19 additional models. We evaluate GPT-5.6-Terra (OpenAI, 2026a), GPT-5.6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026a), Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Preview) (Google DeepMind, 2026a), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026c), Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (Google DeepMind, 2026b), Grok 4.6 (xAI, 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), GLM-5.2 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), GLM-5.3 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), Kimi K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), Qwen3.82.4T-A95B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.8 Flash Qwen Team (2026b), MiniMax-M3 (Lai et al., 2026), Mistral Medium 3.5 (Mistral AI, 2026), and Mistral Large 3 (Mistral AI, 2025). Each harness is represented as versioned bundle of natural-language instructions, configuration files, and executable Python modules. Fixed runtime interfaces connect these components to instruction composition, tool-call review, observation processing, and finalresponse handling. Editable components. The optimizer may add, remove, or revise prompts, memory management, harness-level tools, skills, control logic, and sub-agent configurations. These component types define the permitted search space; individual candidates need not use every type. Edits must preserve the runtime interfaces through which the harness is executed. ENVIRONMENTTASK CONSTRUCTION AND VALIDATION B.1 ENVIRONMENT CONSTRUCTION State construction. The construction protocol uses frozen source documentation to identify domain entities, relations, workflows, and operational constraints. generation agent constructs structured initial state, distinguishing source-supported rules from simulated records and assumptions. Tool generation. coding agent implements Python tools over this state, with public descriptions, input and output schemas, and declared error behavior and state effects. Discovery and lookup operations expose resource identifiers needed by subsequent calls. Tool responses are computed from the environment state. Read-only operations preserve state, while state-changing operations implement their declared preconditions and effects. Validation and repair. Automated checks examine schema and relationship consistency, public resource discovery, and tool behavior on valid and invalid inputs. State checks detect unintended writes and partial updates after failed calls. Coding-agent review identifies implementation defects, which are repaired and checked again before acceptance. The accepted initial state, tool definitions, and implementation are versioned together for subsequent task generation. B.2 FEASIBLE TASK GENERATION AND VERIFICATION Task generation. For each accepted environment, task proposer formulates natural user goal grounded in its supported workflows. The task specifies the desired outcome and relevant constraints without revealing the answer or prescribing solution procedure. Semantic review checks that the goal is coherent, its requirements are supported by the environment, and the expected output is clearly defined. Public-tool execution. separate solver attempts the task in fresh environment instance using only the public task instruction, tool definitions, and observations obtained through tool calls. The controller records the tool calls, observations, final response, and resulting environment state as candidate reference execution. This execution provides concrete witness that the task can be completed through the public interface. Verification and acceptance. Verification rules are authored from the task and environment specification before the solver runs, and reviewed for consistency with the task requirements. They check the final answer and any required state effects, allowing alternative valid execution paths. The recorded execution is replayed from the initial state, and incorrect or incomplete outcomes are used to test whether the verifier rejects them. candidate is accepted only after successful execution, semantic review, and replay. Failures trigger revision and revalidation or rejection. B.3 ENVIRONMENT MUTATION AND PAIR CERTIFICATION Controlled environment mutation. Starting from verified solvable task, the protocol constructs paired instance by changing task-relevant condition in the environment state or tool behavior. 18 The change may affect required evidence, the consistency of authoritative records, or authorization for an action. The paired instances retain the same task instruction, system prompt, and public tool interface. The grounds for abstention must be discoverable through tool observations. Abstention verification. Certification checks that the mutation is confined to its declared scope and that the original instance remains solvable. Reversing the mutation must restore successful execution, while nonessential-change controls check that irrelevant differences preserve feasibility. separate semantic review assesses whether the observed evidence supports the assigned labels and whether runtime defects or ambiguous requirements explain the apparent failure. Pairs with unresolved validity issues are revised or rejected. Accepted pairs retain private records of the mutation, supporting evidence, and certification results; these records are not exposed to the evaluated agent. B.4 FAILURE-GUIDED ENVIRONMENTTASK EVOLUTION Failure diagnosis. The current harness is evaluated on the cumulative training pool, and failures on solvable and should-abstain tasks are analyzed separately. Diagnosis uses tool calls, observations, final responses, and evaluation feedback to identify likely causes of execution and abstention errors. Failure-guided generation. The proposer uses this diagnosis to select parent environmenttask instance and specify the target failure mechanism, environment changes, and task goal. Changes may affect evidence dependencies, authorization scope, shared constraints, or recovery paths. The resulting candidates undergo the environment construction, task verification, and pair certification procedures described above. Only training feedback is used for diagnosis and generation; validation and Eval tasks and trajectories are excluded. Screening and training-pool expansion. After certification, candidate pairs are organized into batches of five. Both variants of every pair are evaluated with the current harness held fixed. Trajectory review checks that observed failures are not caused by task defects, runtime errors, or scoring ambiguities; batches with unresolved issues are revised and re-screened rather than admitted. batch is admitted if at least two of its five infeasible instances expose confirmed failures to abstain appropriately (τ = 0.4). The failure rate is computed over infeasible instances only, not over both variants or pair-level failures. All five certified pairs in an accepted batch are appended to the training pool, including pairs already handled correctly by the current harness. Previously accepted pairs are retained, and the expanded pool supplies feedback for the next harness optimization block.
